'''Leroy Li-Gong Chang''' ({{zh|t=張立綱|p=Zhāng Lìgāng}}; January 20, 1936 – August 10, 2008) was a Taiwanese–American [[electrical engineer]]. Born in China, he studied in Taiwan and then the United States, obtaining his doctorate from [[Stanford University]] in 1963. As a research physicist, he studied [[semiconductor]]s for nearly 30 years at the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] in New York. This period included pioneering work on [[superlattice]] [[heterostructure]]s with Nobel Prize-winning physicist [[Leo Esaki]].

In 1993, Chang moved from New York to Hong Kong, switching from industrial research into academia in anticipation of the [[Transfer of sovereignty over Hong Kong|1997 transfer of the British colony to China]]. He was among the first wave of recruits to the [[Hong Kong University of Science and Technology]]. Over the following 14 years, he helped build the university's reputation in his roles as Dean of Science, Professor of Physics, Vice President of Academic Affairs, and professor emeritus.

Honors bestowed on Chang included memberships of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]], and [[Academia Sinica]] (the national academy of Taiwan). Awards received included the [[James C. McGroddy Prize for New Materials|International Prize for New Materials]] (1985), the [[David Sarnoff Award]] (1990), and the [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] (1993). Chang's death in 2008 was marked with memorial services, and a [[academic conference|symposium]] in his memory was held the following year.

== Early life and education ==
Leroy Li-Gong Chang's family was from [[Jiutai County]], [[Jilin]], in [[Manchuria]], China.{{cn|date=November 2025}} After the [[Japanese invasion of Manchuria]] in 1931, his family escaped to inland China, and Chang was born on January 20, 1936, in [[Kaifeng]], [[Henan]]. His father, {{ill|Zhang Shenfu (engineer)|lt=Zhang Shenfu|zh|张莘夫}}, was a well-known geologist and government official who was assassinated by the [[Communist Party of China|Communists]] in 1946, which prompted the family to move to Taiwan.<ref name=nationalacademies>{{Cite web|title=Leroy L. Chang|url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/26229/chapter/9|publisher=National Academies|access-date=2025-11-02}}</ref> His mother, [[Li Xiangheng]],<ref name=LTC>Leslie T. Chang (2010) [https://books.google.com/books?id=afofrSE_byQC&pg=PT95 ''Factory Girls: Voices from the Heart of Modern China''] p95</ref> was one of the first group of women elected to the [[Legislative Yuan]] in 1948.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://book.yunduan.cn/reader/1866907/1867165 |script-title=zh:老脸霸占万年国会 |work=李敖有话说 |author=Li Ao |language=Chinese |date=9 September 2010 |accessdate=5 February 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130219211648/http://book.yunduan.cn/reader/1866907/1867165 |archivedate=19 February 2013 |author-link=Li Ao }}</ref>

In 1957, Chang graduated with a [[bachelor's degree]] from the Department of Electrical Engineering at [[National Taiwan University]].<ref name="Sinica">{{cite news|title=Academician Leroy L. Chang Passes Away in USA at Age 73|work=Academia Sinica E-news|issue=80|year=2008|publisher=Academia Sinica|url=http://newsletter.sinica.edu.tw/en/news/read_news.php?nid=815|accessdate=5 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304031006/http://newsletter.sinica.edu.tw/en/news/read_news.php?nid=815|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> After serving in the [[Republic of China Armed Forces|Taiwanese Armed Forces]], he immigrated to the United States in 1961 to continue his studies, receiving a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in Electrical Engineering from [[Stanford University]] in 1963.<ref name="obituary"/>

== Career and research ==
=== IBM ===
Between 1963 and 1992, Chang worked at [[IBM]]'s [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] in New York.<ref name="ACAP">{{cite web|title=Leroy Chang|work=Array of Contemporary American Physicists|publisher=American Institute of Physics|url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?changl|accessdate=5 January 2013|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130516024713/http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?changl|archivedate=16 May 2013}}</ref> He held the position of researcher for some twelve years (1963–1968; 1969–1975), with a sabbatical year as Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (1968–1969).<ref>{{cite book|title=Solid state physics in the People's Republic of China: a trip report of the American Solid State Physics Delegation: submitted to the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People's Republic of China|series=Issue 1 of People's Republic of China Series|publisher=National Academies|year=1976|url=https://archive.org/details/solidstatephysic0000amer|url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/solidstatephysic0000amer/page/170 170]|isbn=9780309025232 }}</ref> On his return to IBM research, he spent nine years as manager of its Molecular Beam Epitaxy section (1975–1984). This was followed by seven years as manager of the Quantum Structure section (1985–1992).<ref name="ACAP"/> His research included [[semiconductor physics]], [[2DEG|low-dimensional electron systems]], and [[nanotechnology|nanostructures]].<ref name=Franklin>{{Cite web|title=Leroy L. Chang|date=January 15, 2014 |url=https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/leroy-l-chang|url-status=live|publisher=Franklin Institute|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241221190357/https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/leroy-l-chang|archive-date=2024-12-21|access-date=2025-11-08}}</ref> In the 1970s, he pioneered development of [[quantum well]] and [[Superlattice|superlattice structure]] (SLS) techniques.<ref name="Sinica"/>

One of the key results from Chang's work in this period was using [[molecular beam epitaxy]] to grow [[superlattice]] structures in [[semiconductor]]s. This research was described in a 1973 paper in the ''[[Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology]]'' that was cited multiple times over the following years.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Chang | first1=L. L. | last2=Esaki | first2=L. | last3=Howard | first3=W. E. | last4=Ludeke | first4=R. | last5=Schul | first5=G. | title=Structures Grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy | journal=Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology | publisher=American Vacuum Society | volume=10 | issue=5 | year=1973 | issn=0022-5355 | doi=10.1116/1.1318408 | pages=655–662| bibcode=1973JVST...10..655C }}</ref> Eleven years later, in 1984, this pioneering research paper was featured as a Citation Classic by the [[Institute for Scientific Information|ISI]], an organization that tracks and measures [[impact factor]] and citation frequency and volume for journals and individual research papers.<ref>See {{cite web|last=Garfield|first=Eugene|authorlink=Eugene Garfield|title=Short History of Citation Classics Commentaries|publisher=University of Pennsylvania|url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics.html|access-date=5 January 2013}}</ref> Commentary for this retrospective article was provided by Chang.<ref>{{cite journal|title=This Week's Citation Classic|last=Chang|first=Leroy L.|journal=[[Current Contents]]|issue=12|page=18|date=19 March 1984|publisher=ISI|url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1984/A1984SG00300001.pdf}}</ref> The impact of the research carried out in the 1970s by Chang and his colleagues, including Nobel Prize-winning [[Leo Esaki]] and [[Raphael Tsu]], was highlighted by IBM researchers Theis and Coufal in 2004:

<blockquote>Leo Esaki, Ray Tsu, and Leroy Chang began to envision and investigate designed quantum structures — which are based on interfaces between lattice-matched compound semiconductors — early in the 1970s. Ever since, the study of electronic systems of minute dimensions has ranked among the most exciting areas of condensed-matter physics.<ref>{{cite journal|title=How IBM Sustains the Leading Edge|last1=Theis|first1=Thomas N.|last2=Coufal|first2=Hans J.|journal=The Industrial Physicist|date=April–May 2004|publisher=American Institute of Physics|volume=10|issue=2|page=18|url=http://www.aip.org/tip/INPHFA/vol-10/iss-2/p18.html|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130102231907/http://www.aip.org/tip/INPHFA/vol-10/iss-2/p18.html|archivedate=2013-01-02}}</ref></blockquote>

=== HKUST ===
After 29 years at IBM, Chang moved from industrial research into academia, being appointed the first Dean of Science at the [[Hong Kong University of Science and Technology]] (HKUST) in 1993.<ref name="ACAP"/><ref name="HKUST press">{{cite web|title=HKUST Mourns Passing of Former Vice-President|publisher=Hong Kong University of Science and Technology|date=13 August 2008|url=http://www.ust.hk/eng/news/press_20080813-631.html|accessdate=5 January 2013}}</ref> This was a new university, having been established in 1991. Chang's arrival was described in a 2011 account of the rise of this university: "Other recruits during the first decade included Leroy Chang, a world-renowned experimental physicist from International Business Machines (IBM)."<ref>{{cite book |last=Postiglione |first=Gerard A.  |editor1-first=Philip G.  |editor1-last=Altbach | editor2-first=Jamil | editor2-last=Salmi |title=The Road to Academic Excellence: The making of World-Class Research Universities |publisher=The World Bank |year=2011 |pages=63–100 |chapter=Chapter 3: The Rise of Research Universities: The Case of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology |isbn=978-0821388051|chapter-url=http://siteresources.worldbank.org/EDUCATION/Resources/278200-1099079877269/547664-1099079956815/547670-1317659123740/Chapter3.pdf}}</ref> He held the position of Dean of Science until 1998, when he became Vice President of Academic Affairs—stepping down from this role in 2000. From 1997 until his retirement in 2007, he was also University Professor of Physics.<ref name="ACAP"/>

Chang's departure from New York and arrival in Hong Kong in 1993 was part of a wider influx that saw many leading scientists and researchers taking up positions at universities and institutions in the British colony to be able to take advantage of the opportunities presented by the [[handover of Hong Kong]] in 1997.<ref name="HK1997">{{cite journal|title=Hong Kong's pre-1997 science boom|journal=Science|volume=272|issue=5265|pages=1090–1091|date=24 May 1996|last=Kinoshita|first=June|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-18358036.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150329055609/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-18358036.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=29 March 2015|doi=10.1126/science.272.5265.1090 |via=HighBeam Research|bibcode=1996Sci...272.1090K|s2cid=179028305|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Quoted in an article in 1996, Chang stated:

<blockquote>I would never have come to Hong Kong if it was going to remain just a British colony. We came because of 1997.<ref name="HK1997"/></blockquote>

In addition to his work at HKUST, Chang also supported other science and technology institutions in Hong Kong and the wider region. From 1996 to 1998, he was President of the Hong Kong Institute of Science. In 1998, Chang played a key role in the founding and establishment of the Research Center for Applied Sciences (RCAS) of [[Academia Sinica]] in Taiwan, serving on its advisory committee.<ref name="Sinica"/>

== Family ==
In 1961, during his trip to the United States, Chang met Helen Hsiang-Yung, whom he married the following year. They had two children, Justin and [[Leslie T. Chang|Leslie]].<ref name="obituary">{{Cite newspaper|title=Leroy Chang Obituary |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/sandiegouniontribune/name/leroy-chang-obituary?id=23571811|date=2008-08-17|newspaper=The San Diego Union-Tribune|access-date=2025-11-02}}</ref> Leslie is an author and journalist who is married to [[Peter Hessler]], author of several books about China.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://book.sina.com.cn/news/c/2013-01-21/1412406332.shtml |script-title=zh:从江城过客到中国行者：海斯勒家族的中国情结 |trans-title=Hessler's China Connection |publisher=Sina |language=Chinese |date=21 January 2013 |accessdate=5 February 2013}}</ref>

== Death and tributes ==
Chang died on August 10, 2008, at the age of 72.<ref name=nationalacademies /> Memorial services were held on August 17 in [[El Camino Memorial Park]] in [[San Diego, California]],<ref name="Sinica"/> and at the [[Hong Kong University of Science and Technology]].<ref name="HKUST press"/> A memorial symposium in his honor, 'Recent Advances in Applied Sciences', was held in 2009 at the Academia Sinica.<ref name="RCAS 1">{{cite web|title=Dr. Leroy Chang Memorial Symposium: Recent Advances in Applied Sciences (introduction)|publisher=RCAS, Academia Sinica|url=http://raas09.rcas.sinica.edu.tw/|accessdate=5 January 2013|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303225527/http://raas09.rcas.sinica.edu.tw/|archivedate=3 March 2016}}</ref> The symposium program included "A Tribute to Academician Leroy Chang" and "Remembering Leroy: from SL/QW to RCAS".<ref name="RCAS 2">{{cite web|title=Dr. Leroy Chang Memorial Symposium: Recent Advances in Applied Sciences (program)|publisher=RCAS, Academia Sinica|url=http://raas09.rcas.sinica.edu.tw/program.php|accessdate=5 January 2013|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090508192753/http://raas09.rcas.sinica.edu.tw/program.php|archivedate=8 May 2009}}</ref> At the time of his death, tributes were paid to Chang by his HKUST colleagues, including the university's founding president [[Chia-Wei Woo]]:

<blockquote>Leroy was always exuberant and high-spirited, logical and sensible, forceful and clear, efficient and effective – and always full of wit and humor. As Dean of Science and Vice-President for Academic Affairs, he gave up his beloved and world-renowned scientific career to work totally selflessly towards providing a sound academic environment for his colleagues. HKUST's founding members could not have had a stronger comrade-in-arms in building this new university. I so very deeply mourn his passing.<ref name="HKUST press"/></blockquote>
